newsitem.title: UK: Woolwich debuts in style, promises more cash.
newsitem.headline: Woolwich debuts in style, promises more cash.

text.p: British building society-turned bank Woolwich Plc stormed onto the stock market on Monday, giving shareholders larger-than-anticipated windfalls fuelled by takeover speculation.
Woolwich shares made their debut at 368 pence, giving an average windfall of 2,418 pounds ($4,080), but the stock slipped back during the morning.
The shares were quoted at 338-1/2 pence at 1200 GMT.

Chief executive John Stewart told Reuters a combination of a buoyant market, a strong banking sector and the fact Woolwich was "a very attractive set of businesses" were behind what he admitted was a higher-than-expected price.
Dealers said the price squeeze was the combination of takeover talk in the market and a lack of available stock, but predicted the shares would lose ground.

Analysts had expected the Woolwich, which shed a 150-year mutual tradition to convert to a bank and float on the stock exchange, to debut at around 320 pence, itself far beyond initial estimates of 175-200 pence.

They also said the fundamental valuation for the shares was between 250 and 275 pence, with one recommending holders to get out at current levels if they had received certificates and were able to do so.
"If I had any Woolwich shares at this price, I'd be a seller," said one banking analyst.
But for those Woolwich members -- its savers and borrowers -- who decide to keep their free share allocations, Stewart held out the prospect of a cash handout in a distribution of excess capital.
This, he said, would be in tandem with investments which would improve shareholder returns.
While Woolwich had received a lot of institutional interest for its shares, Stewart said he was hopeful its shareholders would also be its customers.

But around 23.1 percent of the share capital is due to be sold at auction to institutions over the next few days by those shareholders who have decided to take their money and run rather than be long-term investors in the bank.
Stewart said such a drift was inevitable over time but it did not bother him in the slightest.

With an issued share capital of around 1.6 billion shares, Woolwich will have a market capitalisation of around 5.5 billion pounds at the share prices seen on its first day. This will make it one of Britain's top-10 banks and one of the largest quoted companies when it joins the FTSE-100 index in September.
Stewart said Woolwich already had the right balance of diversification in personal financial services and he was confident it could perform well and justify the market's expecations of it.
Woolwich was making headway at reducing its cost base, but this would involve technological improvements rather than job losses or branch closures, Stewart added.
"We are working smarter, not working harder."

And while the bank was taking great care in assessing ways of returning cash to shareholders, Stewart said he could not give a timetable for when this might be or any indication of how much the return would total.
But he expects to be able to put some proposals on the issue to shareholders early next year.
Stewart said Woolwich would weigh up whether it was worth losing a protected status against hostile takeovers by making acquisitions itself if such a move was in shareholders' interests.
But he did not rule out a merger or agreeing to a takeover by a larger firm, if Woolwich was approached.
This was the line the board had adopted since January but no such approach had yet been made, he said, adding he was confident Woolwich could go it alone. ($ = 0.591 British Pounds)
